title: AI Floods Bug Bounties With Junk Reports as Microsoft Pays Record $20 Million
excerpt: Apple caps submissions over AI-generated slop while Microsoft shells out record payouts, as the cybersecurity industry grapples with a double-edged AI revolution.
body:
• Apple has capped bug bounty submissions after a surge of AI-generated vulnerability reports overwhelmed its review system with fabricated bugs.
  • Microsoft paid a record $20 million in bounties to 500 security researchers over the past year, reflecting the growing scale of real vulnerabilities discovered across its platforms.
  • Open-source projects including Curl and GitHub have scrapped or restructured their bounty programs as AI-generated slop drove confirmed-vulnerability rates below 5%.
  • The cybersecurity industry now faces a paradox: AI accelerates both vulnerability discovery and the flood of low-quality reports that bury genuine threats.

The cybersecurity world is caught in an AI-driven paradox. On one side, artificial intelligence is helping researchers discover real vulnerabilities at unprecedented speed. On the other, it is drowning bug bounty programs in fabricated reports that waste engineering time and threaten the survival of programs that keep software safe.

Apple Draws a Line

Apple limited the number of vulnerabilities security researchers can submit to its bug bounty program this week, citing an uptick in reports about fake bugs hallucinated by AI, according to the Financial Times. The company said its review system was processing a high volume of poor-quality submissions from amateur bug hunters using AI tools to locate vulnerabilities that, in many cases, did not actually exist.

The move follows Apple's recent expansion of its bounty program, which now offers up to $2 million for exploit chains comparable to mercenary spyware attacks. The irony is sharp: at the very moment Apple raised the ceiling for genuine discoveries, it was forced to restrict the front door because of junk flooding in.

Microsoft Goes the Other Way

Microsoft, meanwhile, has leaned into the bounty model. The company paid a record $20 million to 500 security researchers worldwide over the past year, an increase from the $13.8 million it paid to 345 researchers the year before. The payout spanned 17 bounty programs covering products from Azure to Dynamics 365.

"Partnering with security researchers through our bug bounty programs is an essential part of Microsoft's holistic strategy to protect customers from security threats."

— Lynn Miyashita, MSRC Technical Program Manager

Microsoft also expanded its AI-specific bounty programs, now offering up to $30,000 for vulnerabilities found in Dynamics 365 and Power Platform AI features. The company recently unveiled Project Perception and MAI-Cyber-1-Flash, agentic defense tools designed to counter the very AI-accelerated exploit development that is reshaping the threat landscape.

Open Source Bears the Brunt

Smaller projects lack the resources to absorb the deluge. The Curl project, a widely used open-source data transfer tool, killed its cash bounty program in January after its confirmed-vulnerability rate fell below 5 percent amid a wave of AI-generated submissions. Maintainer Daniel Stenberg said 20 reports arrived since the start of 2026, placing a high load on the security team, with none identifying an actual vulnerability.

GitHub followed in a similar direction, slashing payouts and imposing signal-based requirements that cap unproven submitters at four reports. The platform acknowledged that tools once meant to assist skilled researchers now let almost anyone generate plausible-looking vulnerability reports at scale.

A Collapsing Window

The pressure is compounded by the speed at which real vulnerabilities are now weaponized. CrowdStrike's H1 2026 report found that AI has collapsed exploitation windows to as little as nine hours in some cases, down from an average of 63 days in 2018. Over 48,000 CVEs were logged in 2025, with 7,400 recorded in June 2026 alone.

Google Chrome patched 1,072 bugs discovered via AI in versions 149 and 150. A Five Eyes advisory warned of exploitation timelines reaching what researchers call negative days — attacks deployed before patches are even published.

What Comes Next

The industry is moving toward a two-tier reality. Well-resourced companies like Microsoft and Apple can absorb higher volumes and pay premium rates for quality discoveries. Smaller projects and open-source maintainers, already stretched thin, are cutting programs entirely or raising bars that may shut out legitimate newcomers alongside the AI noise.

For security researchers, the message is clear: the era of quantity over quality is closing. Programs that survive will reward depth of analysis and working proof-of-concept exploits, not AI-generated guesswork that costs nothing to produce and everything to triage.
